title: Genesis - Creation
author: Jerome (translator)
description: The Latin Vulgate translation of the creation account in Genesis, used throughout the medieval period.

sections.latin: In principio creavit Deus caelum et terram. Terra autem erat inanis et vacua, et tenebrae erant super faciem abyssi: et spiritus Dei ferebatur super aquas. Dixitque Deus: Fiat lux. Et facta est lux. Et vidit Deus lucem quod esset bona: et divisit lucem a tenebris. Appellavitque lucem Diem, et tenebras Noctem: factumque est vespere et mane, dies unus.
sections.translation: In the beginning God created heaven and earth. And the earth was without form and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep: and the Spirit of God moved over the waters. And God said: Let there be light. And there was light. And God saw the light that it was good: and he divided the light from the darkness. And he called the light Day, and the darkness Night: and there was evening and morning, one day.
grammaticalNotes: quod esset bona: indirect statement with subjunctive
factumque est: perfect passive 'and it was made'

sections.latin: Et ait: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram: et praesit piscibus maris, et volatilibus caeli, et bestiis, universaeque terrae, omnique reptili quod movetur in terra. Et creavit Deus hominem ad imaginem suam: ad imaginem Dei creavit illum, masculum et feminam creavit eos. Benedixitque illis Deus, et ait: Crescite et multiplicamini, et replete terram, et subicite eam.
sections.translation: And he said: Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let him have dominion over the fish of the sea, and the fowl of the air, and the beasts, and the whole earth, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth. And God created man in his own image: in the image of God he created him, male and female he created them. And God blessed them, and said: Increase and multiply, and fill the earth, and subdue it.
grammaticalNotes: Faciamus: cohortative subjunctive 'let us make' (divine plural)
theologicalNotes: imago Dei: foundational concept in Christian anthropology
Plural 'Faciamus' debated: royal we, Trinity, or divine council

historicalContext: Jerome's Latin Vulgate (c. 405 CE) became the standard Bible of the Western Church for over a millennium. His translation from Hebrew and Greek aimed for accuracy while maintaining readable Latin.
literaryFeatures: Simple, clear Latin accessible to learners
Formulaic phrases: 'et vidit Deus quod esset bonum'
Historical influence on Western Christianity and Latin literature
